Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
• 65-year-old man with known chronic heart failure presents with 2-week progressive dyspnea (markedly worse past 3 days) and new bilateral ankle edema—consistent with acute decompensation of congestive heart failure.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Worsening shortness of breath over 2 weeks; now breathless walking short distances/around house.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild dry cough; bilateral ankle swelling for 3 days; feels “run-down.”  
• Pertinent negatives: No chest pain, palpitations, fever, orthopnea, or urinary change beyond usual diuretic effect.  
• Past medical history: Chronic heart failure; remote “small” myocardial infarction (~5 yrs ago). No other chronic diseases reported.  
• Medications: Furosemide (1 tab daily – dose unspecified); Aspirin; Bisoprolol.  
• Allergies: Denies drug allergies.  
• Family history: Father MI in early 60s; mother alive with osteoporosis.  
• Social / preventive: Lives alone with two cats; part-time lorry driver (day shifts); ex-smoker (≈1 ppd × 25 yrs, quit); no alcohol; limited exercise.

Examination:
• Clinician reports chest exam, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure “all OK” (exact values not provided).  
• Bilateral ankle edema noted by patient, presumed confirmed on exam.  
• No additional physical findings documented (heart sounds, JVP, lung crackles, weight, etc.).

Impression:
• Primary: Acute decompensated congestive heart failure (high likelihood) – known HF with increased exertional dyspnea and peripheral edema; stable vitals suggest mild–moderate flare.  
• Alternate considerations (per DDx, less likely but to monitor):  
  – Viral/bacterial respiratory infection precipitating HF (dry cough, malaise).  
  – Pulmonary embolism (sedentary work), though history and exam not strongly supportive.

Plan:
• Medication adjustment: Increase Furosemide to 1 tablet twice daily for several days, monitor symptom response.  
• Investigations:  
  – Blood tests today: CBC (anemia), U&E/creatinine (renal function, electrolyte status).  
  – Arrange outpatient echocardiogram within 1–2 weeks to reassess cardiac function.  
• Follow-up: Review in 1 week; earlier if worsening dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, or other concerns.  
• Education / safety-net: Explained signs of deterioration and when to seek immediate help.  
• Work considerations: Acknowledge concern about ability to continue lorry driving; reassess after symptom control.

Quality checks
● Expected but missing: Exact vital signs (HR, BP, RR, SpO₂), weight trends, orthopnea/PND inquiry, medication doses, vaccination status.  
● Conflicts: None significant; brief mishearing of “Bisoprolol” vs “Metoprolol” resolved.  
● Transcript quality: Remote consult; objective data limited, minor audio issues, otherwise coherent.
